paras: The New London sailors' riot was a series of clashes between Black and white sailors in New London, Connecticut, in early June 1919 that ended in a raid by white sailors on a hotel for Black guests and a street battle on Bank Street. Town police and firemen could not stop the fighting, and a detachment of United States Marines restored order. The Black press carried the story through an Associated Negro Press dispatch, which the St. Louis Argus headlined as a riot "Started By Whites."

According to the dispatch, clashes between "Colored and white sailors" had been going on in New London for several days. For some time Black seamen had been protesting that white sailors were attacking them. After one clash, police arrested two white "blue jackets."

The arrested men's comrades demanded their release, and when the police refused, they "sought vengeance." They raided the Hotel Bristol, described as "Colored," threw a large number of its patrons into the street and beat them severely. Reinforcements then arrived for both sides, and a fierce battle developed on Bank Street.
All of the town's police and firemen were unable to stop the riot, so the marines were called in. By "free use of rifle butts," the marines produced what the dispatch called "temporary peace."
The coverage gives no count of the injured, names no victims or attackers, and reports no arrests, inquiry or military discipline after the battle.

The only coverage found was a single Associated Negro Press dispatch, printed with small differences in at least three Black weeklies in mid-June 1919. The St. Louis Argus put it on its front page on June 13 under the headline "Marines Stop Riot Which, Started By Whites, Gets Beyond the Police," placing the blame on the white sailors. A second, badly garbled Argus copy carries a June 13 dateline in an issue indexed as June 6, which suggests a dating error in that copy.

On June 14 the Phoenix Tribune ran the dispatch under the more even-handed headline "Colored and White Sailors Clash in New England," with a June 10 dateline. The Savannah Tribune printed it the same day, dated June 12, inside a column of Associated Negro Press items without a headline of its own. All versions opened with the Black seamen's complaints of attacks by white sailors, framing the raid as the culmination of a pattern rather than a single brawl.

reader.title: New London sailors' riot
bases: White sailors raided a hotel for Black patrons, beat a large number of them, and the clash grew into a street riot between the two groups on Bank Street that police and firemen could not stop (A2, A3, A4).
All four items are copies of one Associated Negro Press dispatch (A1, A2, A3, A4); no independent local or second report was found in the Black press.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press dispatch
accounts.gist: After Black seamen complained of attacks by white sailors and two white sailors were arrested, the arrested men's comrades raided the Hotel Bristol, beat its Black patrons, and a battle on Bank Street followed that only marines could stop.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Argus ran the wire story on its front page under 'Marines Stop Riot Which, Started By Whites, Gets Beyond the Police', placing the blame on the white sailors.
The Phoenix Tribune headlined it 'Colored and White Sailors Clash in New England', and the Savannah Tribune ran it without a headline in an ANP news column.

versions.value: Dateline June 13 (in an issue indexed as June 6)

conflicts.note: All are the same ANP dispatch; the June 6 issue date of A1 cannot carry a June 13 dateline and is likely mis-indexed. The event fell in the days before June 10-12.
The Argus spellings are OCR or typesetting garbles of Bristol.
